chapter_theme: Four songs at Ilanji (இலஞ்சி): pleas that Murugan come on the peacock with Valli at the hour of Death, and that the poet be kept from women's embraces and given the feet; the last is a love-lament for a girl wasting at evening.
structure_note: Two courtesan or lovemaking songs (972, 973), a death-hour plea framed by a portrait of Valli (971), and an akam song in another's voice (974).

971.reading: The first half paints the hunter girl, her eyes, sweet speech, young breasts and elephant-like gait, and asks Murugan to come seated on the peacock with her, clearing the karma of birth, when cruel Death arrives. The praise tells of the Veda lamenting as the little anklets on his feet are worshipped, names him nephew of Vishnu of Srirangam and twelve-armed lord of the hills, and ends at Ilanji where Tamil shines.
971.nuance: The plea itself is only the last line of the first half: பவவினை களைந்து வரு கொடிய அந்தகன் அலவருவாயே, come when Death comes; everything before it describes Valli (எயின்மாது), so the song asks for the divine couple together at death. The opening run of syllables (கரங்க மலமின தரம்ப ...) is hard to divide, and the river with crocodiles and waves that hails him 'Kumara' is not clearly identified.

972.reading: The poet describes lovemaking in detail, earrings shaking, bangles slipping, hair falling loose, sandal paste rubbed away and the waist-cloth slackening as he drowns in the sea of passion, and asks that at that very moment Murugan grant him the vision of his moon-like faces, seated on the blue peacock, and his anklet-bearing feet. The praise names the goddess Sivakami, who dances united with Siva, the one who walked as messenger for Sundarar's song, and calls Murugan the younger brother of the elephant-faced god, the vel against Sura, the meaning of the Veda, and Visakha of Ilanji wedded to the girl of the millet field.
972.nuance: The plea does not ask to escape the embrace but to see Murugan in the middle of it (மூழ்குற்றிடு போது ... அருள்வாயே). சுந்தரர் பாடல் உகந்து இரு தாளைக் கொண்டு நல் தூது நடந்தவர் is Siva going on foot as Sundarar's envoy, named here through the goddess who shares his body.

973.reading: The poet asks that, whirling, wilting and swooning at the spear of women's eyes, he not desire their shoulders, cross the bounds and so waste away and die, and asks for the feet adorned with kadamba, thandai and anklets. The praise names the vel that struck the golden hill, the bridegroom of Indra's daughter, the chest that wedded the girl of the millet field, and the lord who came in the pool as a treasure and dwells at Ilanji.
973.nuance: The plea is built of doubled verbs (சுழன்று சுழன்று துவண்டு துவண்டு), the body acting out its own ruin. The last line plays on இலஞ்சி three times: the pool (the Saravana pond where he was born), இலஞ்சியம (a treasure or refuge), and the shrine.

974.reading: Speaking for a lovesick girl, the singer tells how the evening, the garland, Kama's flower arrows and the burning north wind have stripped her beauty and worn her thin, and asks Murugan to come today, before the tender creeper gives way, so that the love of the breasts once joined may grow. The praise names Murugan who made Death tremble with the vel, walked in the forest and, shame cast aside, pleaded his love to the forest girl, the lord of Ilanji amid groves and paddy, who conquered Sura when even the sun feared him.
974.nuance: This is an akam song, not the poet's own confession: the girl is spoken of in the third person (கோமள வஞ்சி தளராமுன்). Each image is a pun repeated three times, மாலை (evening and garland) and வாடை (north wind, fading, the wind's blast). The praise answers the girl's longing with Murugan's own: he too pleaded with the forest girl (காதல் இரங்கு குமரேசா).

links.note: Both speak for a girl in love with Murugan who wastes at evening under Kama's arrows and the wind; 24 is her mother's lament against the anril bird, the south wind and the crescent, while 974 blames the north wind and asks the god to come today.
